e.t: This noun means “messenger”: someone sent to carry a message or act on behalf of another. It describes a role, not necessarily a particular kind of person, so its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament and related books represented here, the word occurs 269 times, showing that it is a regularly used term for a messenger. Its first recorded occurrence is in Genesis 16:7, and its last is in Susanna 1:60.

This adjective describes someone or something that causes harm or acts unjustly. It can identify conduct that violates what is right, or a person characterized by unfair and injurious behavior. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 96 times, showing a broad use for wrongdoing rather than a narrow reference to one particular offense. Its central sense remains “injurious; unjust,” with the surrounding passage determining how that injustice or harm is expressed.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Azabouch” or “Azavukh.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily its identifying function as a personal name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:16. The available wording does not provide an additional definition or explain the name’s meaning beyond identifying the person who bears it.

This adjective means “in crowds,” describing people or things gathered together in a group rather than appearing individually. It presents something as collective or assembled in numbers. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:14. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains a description of being together in a crowd. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus, without assuming it is the same entity as a Greek New Testament word.

This word is the proper name “Aigyptos,” also rendered “Eyiptos.” It identifies Egypt as a named place in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, rather than describing a general object, action, or quality. As a proper name, its meaning remains tied to the place named in each passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular situation being discussed. It occurs 618 times in the Greek LXX corpus, showing that Egypt is a recurring geographical reference across these writings.

This adjective means “unclean.” It describes someone or something regarded as not clean within the scriptural setting. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly, especially in Leviticus, and appears 158 times across the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. Its recurring use shows a consistent description of uncleanness rather than a single isolated situation. The precise force in any passage depends on what person, object, or condition it describes.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something located at the furthest point or outermost position. It can identify the end or extreme limit of something, rather than its middle or nearer part. The word occurs 32 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Samuel, Kings, and the Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what object, place, or boundary it describes.

This noun refers to education or rearing—the process of bringing someone up and forming them through instruction and care. It describes the upbringing a person receives, rather than a single lesson or isolated act of teaching. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central meaning remains the training and upbringing through which a person is formed.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an accident or a conflict—an adverse event or a clash that brings difficulty. Its two recorded occurrences are both in Sirach, so the word appears only rarely in this Greek Old Testament corpus. The central idea is something going wrong through an unexpected mishap or through opposition between parties. The surrounding passage determines which aspect is intended in a particular verse, but the word itself names the troubling event or confrontation rather than a person or action.

This noun describes something broken off, separated, or abrupt. Its central idea is a sharp ending or a part detached from what it belonged to, rather than something smoothly continuous. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the basic meaning remains the same: something abruptly broken away or cut short.

This adjective means “left,” describing the left side or direction rather than the right. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it is used for physical placement, movement, or orientation. The word occurs 56 times in this Greek LXX corpus, appearing most often in the Old Testament portion, with three occurrences in deuterocanonical books. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it identifies something positioned on, belonging to, or directed toward the left.

Achiel, also rendered Akhil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, both times in 1 Kings: once in 1 Kings 4:6 and again in 1 Kings 16:34. The available information identifies the name but does not provide an underlying definition or a verse narrative. Its significance in either passage therefore comes from the person named and the surrounding context, not from a broader ordinary meaning attached to the name itself.

This is a proper name, referring to “Baithēlitēs” or “Vethilitis.” It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but a specific name used in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This LXX word occurs once, in 1 Kings 16:34. Without the verse text, its precise referent there cannot be identified more specifically, but its lexical function is that of a proper name.

This noun refers to an instrument used for torture or to a chamber where someone is questioned under torture. It names a place or tool associated with severe interrogation, rather than a person or an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording.

Berzellai is a proper name referring to a person. It is rendered as “Berzellai” and also identified as “Verzelle,” so it functions as a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both within Ezra 2:61. The name itself does not provide further meaning about the person’s character or role; those details must come from the surrounding passage and other scriptural references concerning that person.

Gaas is a proper name used to identify someone or something named Gaas, rather than a common word describing a quality, action, or object. Its meaning is therefore centered on the name itself, not on an additional concept or translation idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Joshua 24:31 and Judges 2:9. The available wording preserves it simply as “Gaas,” so no broader ordinary meaning is supported.

This Greek LXX noun means an “engraved figure” or “inscription”—something formed or written by engraving. It can refer to a carved representation or to engraved writing, depending on the sentence. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, including Exodus, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its central idea is a visible mark or figure produced through engraving, rather than a spoken message or an ordinary unmarked object.

“Gomor” is a proper name or designation. It identifies something called Gomor rather than describing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 14 times across 12 verses, with occurrences in Exodus, Ezekiel, 1 Samuel, and Hosea. Its exact referent in any particular verse must be understood from that verse’s surrounding context. The word is first recorded in Exodus 16:16 and last recorded in Hosea 3:2.

This Greek LXX noun means “writing” or “book,” referring to something put into written form or to a written document. It can name a written record rather than an action of writing. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing once each in 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the written item.

This word is a proper name, identified as “Danidan” and also as “Thanithan.” It is a personal or place name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 24:6. The name’s precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This adjective describes someone who is faint-hearted—lacking courage or inner strength when facing difficulty. It functions as a description of a person rather than an action or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. The word’s central idea is a weak or fearful spirit, though the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective describes someone or something as “wretched” or “miserable”—in a deeply unhappy, pitiable, or distressing condition. It is a descriptive word rather than a name or action, so its precise force depends on the person or situation being described. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 5:15, and is rendered “miserable” there. The word’s central idea is a condition deserving pity because of severe distress or ruin.

This Greek LXX verb means “swim across,” describing the action of moving through water from one side to another. It is a concrete action word rather than a description of a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 9:48. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: to cross water by swimming.

This Greek LXX verb means “drive through”: to force or propel something through a place or barrier. It describes an action of passing directly through rather than merely approaching or moving alongside. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 11:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains movement driven through something.

This noun means “double measure,” referring to a measure understood as twofold or twice the ordinary measure. It names a quantity or standard of measurement rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in 2 Kings 7. Its precise significance in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse and the thing being measured.

This word refers to a young gazelle—a small, graceful animal. It is a noun naming the animal itself, not an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 13:14, and is rendered “fawn.” The wording “little gazelle” highlights its youthful size and kind. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about the animal; the word itself identifies the creature.

This is a proper name, rendered “Ezekiou” or “Ezekiu.” It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 22 times in this Greek LXX corpus, across 22 verses, from 2 Kings through 2 Maccabees. Its exact reference in any passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, since the name itself chiefly identifies the person.

This verb means “hurdle” or “burst in,” describing a forceful movement into or over something. It presents action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 5:19, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The core idea remains a sudden, vigorous movement—either leaping over an obstacle or pressing rapidly into a place. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation corpus.

“Modelling in relief” refers to a raised decorative design, such as an image or pattern formed so it stands out from a surface. This noun describes the finished relief work rather than an action or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 6:35, so its meaning is especially focused: it names a kind of crafted, three-dimensional ornamentation. The surrounding verse supplies the specific object and setting; the word itself points to the relief technique or design.

To free someone or something means to release it from bondage, restraint, or control. This Greek LXX verb expresses the action of making free, rather than freedom as an abstract condition. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, both times in 2 Maccabees. The basic sense remains simple: a person or group is freed from an imposed condition. The surrounding verse determines who is freed and from what.

This word refers to information being made known, or to a disclosure. It describes the communication of something that was previously not known, so its central idea is the revealing or reporting of information. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:9. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely what information is being disclosed there, but the word itself points to the act or content of making something known.

This Greek LXX verb means “erase; wipe out.” It describes removing something so that it is no longer present or counted. The word is used 45 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, so its basic sense applies across repeated scriptural settings rather than to one isolated passage. The precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being removed, but the central idea remains complete erasure or removal.

This Greek LXX verb means “come on/against”: it describes someone or something approaching, arriving, or moving toward another, sometimes with the sense of coming against an opponent. It is an action word, so its precise force depends on what or whom the movement is directed toward. The word occurs 105 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing regular use for coming upon or approaching people, situations, or places. [p03:word:lxx:L705068:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705068:occurrences]

This adjective describes something that is “one in ten”—a quantity or portion consisting of one part for every ten. It identifies a proportion rather than a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times across 15 verses, especially in passages concerning measured portions and offerings. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the noun or phrase it describes, but its central idea remains a tenth or one part out of ten.

gl: utter words ominous of the event
d: utter words ominous of the event

e.t: This verb means to utter words that are ominous about an event. It describes speech that points toward a troubling or threatening outcome, without by itself explaining whether the speaker is warning, predicting, or commenting on what will happen. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Deuteronomy and Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is speaking in a way marked by ominous reference to an event.

This word means “hoopoe,” the name of a particular bird. It functions as a noun in the Greek Old Testament and identifies the bird itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, across Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Zechariah. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines what is being said about the bird in that specific passage.

Ephrōn, also rendered Efron, is a personal name rather than a word describing an idea or action. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. The name occurs 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing most often in Genesis and also in Joshua, 2 Chronicles, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Its meaning here is therefore the person’s name itself; the surrounding passage identifies which Ephrōn is intended in each occurrence.

“Zabdiou; Zavthiu” is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:21. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the verse text or wider passage, its personal identity and role cannot be explained further here. The word functions simply as a person’s name in that occurrence.

This verb describes strong, devoted feeling or action, expressed as being “zealous” or “jealous.” It can refer to energetic commitment toward a person or cause, or to intense concern over a relationship or loyalty. The surrounding context determines which emphasis is intended. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 44 times, so it is used across a range of situations rather than carrying only one narrow emotional shade. Its core idea is ardent concern that moves a person to act.

This verb means “leaven” or “leavened.” It refers to the action or result of causing dough to rise through leaven. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Exodus and once in Hosea, and both occurrences are rendered “leavened.” Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning concerns dough changed by leavening.

Thaath is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is preserved as a personal name rather than translated into a descriptive meaning. The name appears three times in the Greek text of the Old Testament, all in genealogical lists in 1 Chronicles. Because the available passages do not provide a definition or explanation of the name itself, its ordinary lexical significance is simply the personal name Thaath. Its precise identification in any occurrence depends on the surrounding genealogy.

This verb means “pressure; press against.” It describes applying force to something or someone, or being pressed by an opposing force. The basic idea is pressure that bears down, constrains, or pushes against a person or object. It occurs 91 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented in this LXX corpus, so it is used across many passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX noun means “altar,” referring to the designated structure used in biblical worship. It names an altar rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 413 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, showing that it is a recurring term for this worship-related object. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Iani is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader gloss; its supplied meaning is simply “Iani.” This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 5:12. Without the verse text or wider passage, the name alone does not establish the person’s role, character, ancestry, or significance. Its basic function is to identify an individual named Iani.

Idouma is a proper name, represented in the Greek Old Testament by “Idouma” and “Ithuma.” It does not function as an ordinary descriptive word with a general English meaning. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. The two recorded references are Genesis 25:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:30. Its precise identification and significance in either passage depend on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek Old Testament noun refers to a “sacrifice” or a “festival.” It can name either the sacrificial offering or the appointed festival occasion itself. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Kings 10:20, so its broader range is limited to this single recorded use. Its basic meaning remains centered on something set apart as a sacrifice or a festival.

gl: set a going; put in motion
d: set a going; put in motion

e.t: This Greek verb means “set a going” or “put in motion.” It describes causing something to move, begin, or proceed. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, so it is an established action word within this corpus rather than a personal name or abstract idea. Its precise sense in a particular sentence depends on what is being moved or started there.

This adjective means “fruitful,” describing something that produces fruit or yields a productive result. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Genesis 1:11–12. Its basic sense is therefore connected with bearing or producing fruit, while the surrounding passage determines what is being described. It is an adjective, so it characterizes a living thing, plant, land, or other subject as fruitful rather than naming the fruit itself.

καταναγκάζω means to overpower someone by force or to confine them. It describes an action that removes a person's freedom through coercion, either by forcing submission or by keeping the person under restraint. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) material represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 2:15. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine which aspect—forceful compulsion or confinement—is emphasized there.

This Greek LXX verb means “arrive” or “come down to.” It describes movement toward a destination or the point at which someone reaches a place or situation. The word appears five times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here: once in the Old Testament and four times in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one passage depends on what destination or outcome the surrounding sentence identifies.

This Greek LXX verb means “settle.” It describes taking up residence or coming to live in a place, rather than merely passing through. The word is broadly used across the Greek Old Testament and related writings, occurring 580 times, so its basic sense covers people or groups establishing themselves in a location. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on settling somewhere, dwelling there, or remaining established. It is not limited to one particular kind of inhabitant or setting.

This word means “millet,” a small cultivated grain used as food. It is a noun naming the grain itself, rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 4:9. That single occurrence identifies the word’s ordinary lexical sense, while the surrounding verse and passage determine its particular role there. The word therefore refers simply to millet within this corpus, without requiring an expanded symbolic or theological meaning.

This word means a “sheath” or “scabbard”—a protective covering made to hold a sword or other blade when it is not being used. As a noun, it names the container or covering itself, rather than the weapon inside it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its repeated use in these passages keeps the meaning concrete: a sheath is associated with carrying, storing, or putting away a sword.

This noun means “groundwork,” referring to the base or supporting foundation on which something rests or is built. It points to what provides stability and support, rather than to a finished structure itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, across Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Joel, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a firm underlying base.

This proper name refers to the Lydoi, also given as Lithi. It identifies a people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs three times: once in Jeremiah and twice in Ezekiel. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here. The name appears in Jeremiah 26:9, Ezekiel 27:10, and Ezekiel 30:5.

Masphar is a proper name, also rendered Masfar. It identifies a named person or group in the Greek Old Testament, but the available wording does not establish which one. The name occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Ezra 2:2 and once in Nehemiah 7:7. Both occurrences use the rendering “Masphar.” Its precise identification depends on the surrounding lists and passage context rather than on the name itself.

This adjective describes something as “brimming; full”—filled to a substantial or overflowing extent. It can describe a person, object, or condition that has reached fullness, with the surrounding sentence showing what is full and how that fullness matters. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, across Esther, Proverbs, Ezekiel, and Nahum. Its basic idea remains straightforward: something is filled up or abundantly supplied rather than empty or lacking.

This word means “mother,” referring to a woman in relation to her child. It is a noun used for the ordinary family relationship of motherhood in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures. The word appears 292 times in the LXX corpus, showing broad and repeated use across its books. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a child’s mother or maternal parent.

Miron is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 18:26. Because names identify people and this name has no supplied descriptive definition, its meaning is simply the person designated by Miron in that passage. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person’s role or place in the passage; the name itself does not communicate an additional quality or message.

Michael is a proper name, rendered “Michaēl” or “Mikhel.” It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 13 times across 13 verses, including genealogical lists and other passages where the name distinguishes a particular person. Its exact reference may identify different individuals, so the surrounding verse is needed to know which Michael is meant. [p03:word:lxx:L708953:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L708953:occurrences]

Mosoath is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than as a descriptive word, so its meaning is the designation “Mosoath” itself. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 23:13. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain whether the name refers to a person, place, or other named subject.

This word refers to someone or something detained—held back or kept in custody rather than free to leave. It is a noun, so it identifies the person or thing being detained, not the act of detaining. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 21:8. Its lexical meaning is clear, but the verse’s precise force depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This word means “eighty,” the cardinal number that comes after seventy-nine and before eighty-one. It functions as an indeclinable number, so it identifies a quantity or count rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 37 times across 36 verses. Its use ranges from expressing ages and counts to stating quantities in historical or administrative passages. The surrounding verse determines what is being counted, but the word itself consistently identifies the number eighty.

This noun means “happiness” or “bliss”: a state of deep well-being and joy. It names the condition of being truly happy rather than an action or command. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 30:15. The surrounding verse is needed to determine how this broad idea is applied there, but the word itself points to positive, flourishing well-being. Its meaning is therefore best understood as happiness or bliss in the ordinary sense of a deeply blessed condition.

This Greek LXX word means “in back; after.” It describes something located behind another thing, or something occurring later than it. As an adverb, it can indicate position or direction; as a preposition, it can show that one person or thing is behind or follows another. The word occurs 346 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its precise English wording depends on how it functions in each sentence.

This adverb means “at all” or “universally,” expressing an idea that applies completely, without exception, or in the fullest possible extent. It can strengthen a statement by showing that something is true in every case or in any sense under consideration. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs only twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the sentence and surrounding context.

This verb means to disdain—to regard someone or something with contempt or to treat it as unworthy of respect. It describes an active attitude or response rather than simply noting that something is unimportant. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding wording determines whether the disdain is directed toward a person, a claim, or something valued, but the central idea remains rejection rooted in contempt. Its four occurrences span 4 Maccabees 6:9, 7:16, 8:28, and 14:1.

This noun refers to an ape or monkey. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 9:21, and describes an animal rather than a person, place, or abstract idea. The wording identifies the creature plainly; its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word’s basic meaning remains stable as a name for this kind of animal.

This Greek LXX noun describes something that entangles or catches the feet, creating a hindrance to walking or movement. Its concise meaning is “foot-entangling.” It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 4:16. The word’s basic sense identifies an object or feature that can trip, catch, or hinder someone’s feet; the exact referent in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “sea,” referring to a large body of salt water. It is a noun, so it names the waters themselves rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 15:5. The word’s basic meaning remains straightforward: it identifies the sea as a place or natural feature. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This verb means “do before”: it describes carrying out an action earlier than something else or taking an action in advance. It is an action word, so its focus is on what someone does beforehand, not on a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 6:27. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what action is being described there.

Reoum, also known as Rheum, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the LXX, at Ezra 2:2. Because the name is preserved as a name and no ordinary definition is given, its meaning is best understood as the person’s designation, not as a quality, action, or abstract idea. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s role there.

This Greek LXX verb means “whistle”: to produce or express a whistling sound. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Song of Songs 4:15. That reference identifies its only recorded occurrence in this corpus, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular use there. Its central meaning remains the act of whistling.

Sagaph, also rendered Sagaf, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles 2, at 1 Chronicles 2:47 and 2:49. The name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character, role, or significance; those details depend on the surrounding genealogical context.

Salōmōnta is a proper name, referring to a person named Salomonta. It is not a descriptive word such as a title, action, or character quality; its function is to identify an individual. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 18:16. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, the name itself does not establish further details about the person or the significance of the reference.

Sauas, also rendered Savas, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:3. The available wording gives the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its meaning. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and family-list context, which are handled separately.

Serada is a proper name, also rendered Seratha, identifying a person or place named in the Greek Old Testament. Its precise referent cannot be determined from the available lexical information alone. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 13:19, and is preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. The wording itself does not supply a broader symbolic or conceptual meaning beyond this named designation.

This adjective means “fattened.” It describes a person or animal that has been made fat or well-fed, emphasizing a resulting condition rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in 1 Kings 5:3 and Jeremiah 26:21. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the condition of being fattened.

gl: flour of spelt mixed and made into dough
d: flour of spelt mixed and made into dough

e.t: This noun refers to spelt flour that has been mixed with water or another liquid and made into dough. It describes a basic prepared food, not merely dry grain or flour by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears four times, including references in Exodus, 2 Samuel, and Jeremiah. Its ordinary meaning remains practical and concrete: a quantity of spelt flour prepared for baking or cooking. The surrounding verse determines how that dough functions in each passage.

This adjective describes something that is flexible or pliant—able to bend rather than being rigid. It is a physical description, used in the Greek Old Testament for objects or materials that can be shaped or bent. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, across Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and Esther. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what object or material the surrounding passage describes.

This word is the personal name “Simeon,” identifying a person rather than describing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it appears as a proper name across genealogical and historical passages. It occurs 52 times in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees, showing continued use as a person’s name rather than an ordinary vocabulary term.

This adverb means “by heaps” or “in heaps,” describing something arranged, gathered, or occurring in piles or large accumulated groups. It tells how something is present or happens rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 18:23. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a heap-like or piled arrangement. Its supplied meaning is straightforward and concrete: things are present in heaps rather than singly or in a scattered way.

This word means “three hundred.” It is an adjective used to describe a quantity or number, identifying something as consisting of three hundred units, people, animals, or other counted items. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 71 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 3 Maccabees. Its precise connection to the thing being counted depends on the surrounding verse, but the numerical sense remains consistent: a total of three hundred.

This word describes someone or something as being three years old. It functions as a verb, expressing the state of having reached that age rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, with three occurrences in Genesis and one in 1 Samuel. Its basic meaning remains focused and specific: it identifies an age of three years. The surrounding verse determines whether the word describes a person, animal, or another subject, but the age itself is plainly defined by the word.

This word means “officer,” referring to a person who serves in an official position or carries out duties under authority. As a noun, it identifies the person rather than the action being performed. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs four times, appearing in Proverbs, Isaiah, Daniel, and Wisdom. Its precise role in any one passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is a recognized servant or official entrusted with responsibilities.

This Greek LXX verb means to harbor or entertain someone—to receive and care for a person, often by offering welcome or shelter. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, in 1 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is receiving someone hospitably or giving them a place of refuge.

This noun means a vessel, specifically a pitcher—an object used to hold or pour something. It names a physical container rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 52:19. The word’s basic meaning remains straightforward: a pitcher or similar vessel. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

Phakee (also rendered Fakee) is a proper name—the personal name preserved in this Greek Old Testament wording. It does not describe an action, quality, or general object; it identifies someone by name. The name occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, in 11 verses, chiefly in 2 Kings, and also in 2 Chronicles and Isaiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse, but the word itself functions as a name rather than a common noun.

This Greek LXX adverb describes something done or experienced in a fearful or frightening way. It can express the manner in which an action occurs, emphasizing fear, awe, or alarm rather than naming the person or thing involved. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including once in Psalms and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its action. The central idea remains that something happens fearfully or in a way that causes fear.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “bristle”: to become stiff or stand up, expressing a physical reaction of bristling. It appears only twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Job and once in Jeremiah. The word itself describes the act or state of bristling, while the surrounding verse determines what produces that reaction and how the image functions in context.

This verb describes someone as “favored” or “gracious.” It expresses the idea of receiving favor or being treated graciously, depending on how the sentence presents the action. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 18:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense concerns favor and gracious treatment rather than a general description of kindness.

This word means “swallow,” the name of a small bird. It is a noun used for the bird itself, rather than an action such as swallowing food. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its meaning remains consistent across these occurrences: it identifies a swallow as part of the natural world described in the text.

This word refers to a rabbit or coney, a small animal. It is a noun naming the creature rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:26. The word’s basic meaning is therefore the animal itself; the particular significance of its mention depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its recorded use is limited to this single occurrence in the Greek Old Testament.

This Greek LXX verb means “strip bare” or “pluck off,” describing the act of removing something from its covering or attachment. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 44:20. The precise force of the verb in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is physical removal.
